claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys is governed primarily by high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy enforces a uniform, single-phase atomic distribution.
A uniform, single-phase atomic distribution retards phase segregation.
A uniform, single-phase atomic distribution retards surface reconstruction.
The initial nanoalloy is single-phase and compositionally homogeneous at ambient conditions.
An inert atmosphere minimizes external oxidation during high-temperature treatment.
Enhanced configurational entropy increases the energy barrier for atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
Increasing the barrier to atomic diffusion and rearrangement impedes phase segregation and chemical instability.
The homogeneous nanoalloy state is kinetically trapped and can be preserved during heating.
At high temperature, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single phase and show less elemental segregation than lower-configurational-entropy controls.
Lower-entropy analogues lack sufficient entropy stabilization to resist diffusion-driven phase separation.
The stabilization effect holds only below a critical temperature threshold.
Above the critical threshold, thermal energy overcomes the configurational-entropy barrier and causes observable phase segregation.
Surface oxidation and element-specific segregation are plausible alternative mechanisms governing nanoalloy instability.
Modifying elemental ratios can produce a controlled reduction in configurational entropy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes configurational entropy as enforcing a uniform single phase, suggesting thermodynamic stabilization, while the mechanism describes the same state as kinetically trapped through an increased diffusion barrier. Thermodynamic stabilization and kinetic trapping are distinct explanations and are not reconciled.

The main hypothesis says configurational entropy is the primary governor of stability, whereas the falsification rule tests whether it uniquely governs stability. Similar behavior in the two controls would reject uniqueness but would not necessarily falsify a weaker claim of primary influence.
